transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Well, honestly, I'm just having the hardest time lately. It's my job, mostly. I work at this big distribution warehouse, you know, moving freight and doing inventory, and I've been doing this kind of work for a long time, ever since I took some classes at the community college years ago and realized sitting at a desk just wasn't for me. 

But lately... I just can't keep my mind on one single thing anymore. It's like my brain is a pinball machine. I'll be right in the middle of a stock count, looking right at the boxes, and then—beep beep beep—a forklift alarm goes off three aisles over, and my head just snaps to it. Or a pager goes off, or someone is just moving a pallet of materials near the loading dock, and suddenly I'm completely pulled off my count. I'll just stand there watching them move the pallet, thinking about where it's going or who's driving, and then by the time I look back at my clipboard, I've completely lost my place. 

And the worst part is, I don't even realize I've messed up until later when I see I've put all the wrong numbers into the inventory system. It's causing a real mess, you know? My supervisor has to come back and ask me why the counts are off, and I have to go re-count the whole section, and I just... I don't know why every little noise is dragging my attention away like this. It's a warehouse, it's always loud, but now it's like I hear every single beeper and alarm all at once and I just can't filter any of it out to do my actual job.
Do you find yourself getting distracted like this at work is the only place, or does it also happen in other areas of your life?

Well, you know, now that you mention it... I guess I really haven't noticed it happening anywhere else. I mean, it's mostly just at the warehouse because that's where I need to focus, you know? When I'm at home, I live alone, so it's pretty quiet. I just watch my shows—mostly those home renovation ones, I love seeing how they tear down the walls and make everything open concept—and I don't really have to concentrate on much. 

Sometimes I'll be cooking dinner, maybe making a pot roast or just boiling some pasta, and the phone might ring, but that's normal to get distracted by a phone, right? It's not like the warehouse where there are a hundred things happening at once. I mean, my sister called the other day while I was making a salad, and I stopped to talk to her for a good forty-five minutes about her daughter's new dog—a golden retriever mix, real cute, but apparently it chews on the baseboards—and I forgot I was even making the salad until I hung up. But I think anyone would do that, don't you? 

So, yeah, I'd say it's really just the job. That's where the noise is. The beeping, the clanking, the guys yelling across the floor about where the pallets are supposed to go. It's just so overwhelming there right now. At home, or when I'm out at the grocery store, I just get my list and get my things. I don't feel that same... pulling away of my brain, if that makes sense. It's just that warehouse environment that's really doing a number on me lately.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others or blurting out answers before they finish speaking?

No, I wouldn't say I do that. I mean, I try to be polite, you know? My mother always raised me to let people finish their sentences. She used to say, "God gave you two ears and one mouth for a reason," which I always thought was a little cliché, but she meant well. 

I mean, sure, sometimes if I'm talking to my sister and she's going on and on about that dog of hers—like I was telling you before, the one that chews the baseboards—I might jump in just to agree with her or say, "Oh, I know, that sounds awful," but I'm not really interrupting her to take over the conversation, you know? It's more just participating. 

And at work, well, nobody really talks to each other in full sentences anyway. It's too loud. You just yell, "Hey, pallet jack!" or "Watch your back!" and that's the end of it. There's not much of a conversation to interrupt in the first place. When my supervisor talks to me, like when he's asking why my inventory counts are off because I got distracted by the forklift alarms, I just stand there and listen. I don't try to cut him off or make excuses before he's done. I just wait until he's finished and then tell him I'll go fix it. So, no, I really don't think I have a problem with blurting things out or talking over people. I'm usually pretty good about waiting my turn to speak.
Do you often find yourself acting on impulses, like doing things without thinking them through?

Well, um... I guess maybe a little bit? Not like crazy things, but... well, okay, so there's this craft market that sets up downtown on the first weekend of every month. It's really nice, they close off the street and all these local artisans come out. And lately, I don't know, I just get these ideas in my head. Like last month, I saw this booth with all these beautiful hand-painted ceramic tiles, and suddenly I just knew—I absolutely knew—I was going to redo my entire kitchen backsplash myself. 

I've never tiled anything in my life, mind you, but I just felt this rush of energy about it. So I bought, oh gosh, I don't even want to say... I bought boxes of these tiles. And then I went to the hardware store and bought all the grout, the spacers, the special trowels, even a wet saw. A wet saw! I live in a small apartment, where am I even going to use a wet saw? But in the moment, it just made perfect sense. I was going to be this master DIYer. I spent hours looking at different shades of grout—did you know there are like fifty shades of white grout? 

And then the next weekend, I got it in my head that I was going to start painting landscapes. I went to the art supply store and just started grabbing things. Professional-grade oils, canvases, a whole set of palette knives, these beautiful, expensive wooden frames... I was so sure I was going to paint these masterpieces and maybe even sell them at the market myself. 

But now... well, the tiles are just sitting in boxes in my living room, stacked up next to the TV, and the paints are still in the shopping bags. I haven't touched any of it. And when I got my credit card bill last week, I just... I actually cried a little. I spent way, way more than I should have. More than I can really afford on my warehouse salary, to be honest. I'm just so embarrassed looking at that balance, knowing all that money went into things that are just gathering dust. I don't know why I do it, I just get so swept up in the idea and I swipe my card before I even think about how I'm going to pay for it later.
Do you often feel restless or fidgety, like you need to get up and move around?

Well, I wouldn't say I'm pacing around the warehouse floor or anything like that. When I'm at work, I'm moving constantly anyway, lifting boxes, pulling pallets, walking back and forth from the loading dock to the staging area. It's physical work, so you'd think I'd be absolutely exhausted by the end of the day, right? Most of the guys I work with, they clock out and they just want to go home, crack open a beer, and melt into their recliners. And honestly, that used to be me, too. I'd come home, make a quick sandwich, and just crash on the sofa in front of the TV. 

But lately... it's like my body doesn't get the memo that the shift is over. I come home and I'm just buzzing. Like there's this electricity humming right under my skin. Sitting on the couch feels completely impossible. I'll try to sit down to watch one of my renovation shows, and my leg will start bouncing, or I'll feel this tightness in my chest like I just have to get up and *do* something. 

So instead of resting, I've been finding all these projects around the apartment. The other night, after an eight-hour shift, I came home and completely reorganized my kitchen cabinets. And I don't mean just straightening up—I took everything out, wiped down the shelves, put down new contact paper—that pretty floral kind I found on sale at the discount store—and then put all the cans and boxes back in alphabetical order. Alphabetical! Who does that? And when I ran out of things to do in the kitchen, I went out to the little detached garage I rent and started sorting through all these old plastic storage bins I haven't opened in years. I was out there until 2:00 in the morning, just sorting old winter clothes and holiday decorations, feeling like I had all the energy in the world. So, yeah, I guess you could say I'm feeling pretty restless, just... mostly when I'm supposed to be relaxing.
Are you finding it difficult to maintain your relationships with family and friends due to your current struggles at work?

Well, it definitely is spilling over, yes. I mean, work has been... well, you remember I mentioned my inventory counts being off before? It’s gotten to the point where I’m constantly having to go find my supervisor—Dave, he's a nice enough guy, but he's got a lot on his plate with the regional shipping quotas right now—and I have to double-check everything with him because I keep making these silly inventory errors. I'll write down 40 boxes of brackets instead of 400, or I'll put the wrong staging lane on the manifest, and I just have to keep going back to him to fix it or have him check my math. It’s embarrassing, having to ask him to look over my shoulder like I’m some brand new hire when I’ve been doing this for years. 

And then, you know, I bring all that frustration home with me, or maybe I’m just so wound up from the day, and it’s really taking a toll on things with my husband. He just retired a few months ago. He was a machinist for over thirty years, worked incredibly hard, on his feet all day just like me, and this was supposed to be our time to kind of figure out this new phase of life. You know, settling into his retirement, enjoying the slower pace, maybe just having a quiet cup of coffee together in the morning. 

But instead of that, we are just constantly arguing. It’s like we can’t even be in the apartment together without snapping at one another. He’ll ask a simple question about dinner, or sigh about those boxes of tiles I still have sitting next to the TV, and I just completely bite his head off. It’s gotten to the point where it feels like we’re just walking around each other all the time. We're just tiptoeing around our own home, staying in separate rooms just to avoid setting off another argument, instead of actually enjoying his retirement. It breaks my heart, honestly, because he deserves a peaceful time right now, and I just... I can't seem to give that to him with how scattered I am at work and how tense I am at home.
Do you have trouble waiting in lines or for your turn in general?

Waiting in lines? No, um, I wouldn't say that. I actually don't mind waiting at all. It's funny, because you'd think with how wired I get at home, I'd be jumping out of my skin in a checkout line, but it's really not like that. 

Like, my husband, bless his heart, he cannot stand a line. If we go to the grocery store—we usually go to the big grocery store over on 4th Street because they actually have decent produce, not like those rock-hard pale tomatoes you get at the discount mart—anyway, if there are more than two people in front of us at the checkout, he starts huffing and puffing. He'll be looking around, shifting his weight, trying to find another lane, muttering under his breath about how they need to open more registers. 

But me? I'm perfectly fine. It's almost like... I don't know, a forced break, you know? I'll just stand there with my cart and look at the magazines on the rack. I never buy them, of course, they're like six or seven dollars for a single magazine now, which is just absolute robbery if you ask me, but I'll read the celebrity headlines or look at the baking pictures. It's peaceful, in a weird way. 

And it's the same at the warehouse, too. If I'm waiting for one of the forklift drivers—usually it's Gary, he's a little slow but he's very safe, never drops a load—if I'm waiting for him to clear a pallet so I can get in there and move my freight, I just wait. I'll lean against a support beam and just wait my turn. He'll apologize for the hold up, and I always just wave him off and say, 'Take your time, Gary, I'm getting paid by the hour.' 

So, no, waiting my turn isn't really a problem. I can be very patient when I have to be, whether it's at the store or the DMV or wherever. It's really just when I'm at home and supposed to be relaxing on my own time that I get all keyed up and can't seem to sit still. But put me in a line? I'll stand there as long as it takes.
Do you find it hard to finish tasks that you start, like leaving them incomplete or having to come back to them later?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. And honestly, that's really what brings me in here to see you in the first place, because I just... I can't seem to keep my mind on one thing anymore. It's like my brain just won't let me finish what I start. 

Especially at work. I know I mentioned those inventory errors earlier, the ones I have to keep taking to Dave to fix? Well, the reason they're happening is exactly that—I can't finish the task. I'll start counting a section, you know, clipboard in hand, really trying to focus, but the warehouse is just so full of noise and lately every single little thing completely derails me. I'll be halfway through counting a stack of boxes, and then a beeper will go off on the loading dock, or one of the forklift alarms will start up—you know that loud, piercing *beep-beep-beep* when they throw those things in reverse?—or even just someone moving a wooden pallet a few aisles over. It makes this loud scraping sound on the concrete. 

And the second I hear it, it's like my brain just drops whatever I was doing. I get pulled completely off the count. I'll turn to look, or I'll start thinking about what truck Gary is loading, or I'll literally just walk away from my staging lane to see what the noise was, leaving my own work completely unfinished. And then, by the time I finally wander back to my clipboard, I've totally lost my place. I'll think I finished the section when I actually only counted the first two rows, and then I realize later I've put the completely wrong numbers into the inventory system. 

It's just so frustrating. I'm leaving things half-done all day long because every little noise just yanks my attention away. I used to be able to focus through a hurricane, you know? I could tune out all those alarms and beepers and just get my freight moved. But now it's like every sound is a shiny object and I just drop what I'm doing to look at it.
Do you have trouble organizing your time and prioritizing tasks?

Organizing my time? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, if anything, I'm the most organized person I know. You kind of have to be in freight, you know? You can't just wing it when you've got three different trucks waiting at the loading docks and a staging area that's already full from the night shift. 

I always know exactly what needs to happen and in what order. Like, I'll get in at 5:45—I always like to be fifteen minutes early to get my coffee and put my lunch in the breakroom fridge, because if you don't get it in there early, the second shift guys will just shove your Tupperware all the way to the back and it gets frozen against the cooling coils—but anyway, I get my clipboard and I know right away: okay, the rush orders for the downtown stores have to be processed first, then the backstock needs to be rotated, and only then do I do the inventory counts. I know exactly how to prioritize. 

And it's the exact same way at home, too. I am the absolute keeper of the schedule. I have this big magnetic calendar on the side of the refrigerator. I actually went to the office supply store a few years ago and bought a special pack of fine-tip dry erase markers just for it, because the thick ones just turn into a smudgy mess. I use blue for my husband's things—like his physical therapy for his knee, or when he's going over to his brother's house—and green is for when the utility bills are due, and red is for my work shifts. I even plan out our meals for the week on Sunday afternoons so we don't end up just staring into the pantry at six o'clock every night. 

So, no, figuring out what to do or managing my time isn't the issue at all. I know exactly what my priorities are. It's just like I was saying a minute ago... it's just that once I actually *start* the priority task, my brain gets hijacked by every little beep or scrape on the floor and I wander off. But the actual planning and organizing part? I've got that down to an absolute science. I've always been a very structured person, so I don't have any trouble with that part of things.
Do you often find yourself saying or doing things in social situations that you later regret?

Saying or doing things I regret? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I'm pretty careful about how I talk to people, actually. I've always been one to think before I speak, you know? 

I mean, working in a warehouse, you get all types. You get the guys who just curse up a storm over every little thing, or the ones who make inappropriate jokes in the breakroom—like this one guy, Lenny, who used to work the docks, he was always saying things that made you want to just roll your eyes and walk away. But I never engage in that kind of stuff. I keep things professional. I'll ask about people's weekends, or talk about the weather, or maybe mention a recipe I tried, but I don't go blurting out things that are going to upset anybody or cause drama. 

And even with my husband, we've been married for thirty-two years, and sure, we bicker sometimes, like anyone does. He'll leave his shoes right in the middle of the hallway where I trip over them, and I'll tell him he needs to put them in the closet. But I don't fly off the handle and say terrible things that I have to apologize for the next day. I'm just not wired that way. I'm generally a very level-headed person when it comes to dealing with other people. 

Even now, with my mind feeling so scattered and jumping around at every noise, I'm still polite. I'm still myself. If I wander away from my clipboard because Gary dropped a pallet too hard, I don't go over there and yell at him or say something rude. I just kind of look, realize I got distracted, and then feel embarrassed about my own brain, you know? But I don't lash out or say things I wish I hadn't. So, no, social situations are fine. I don't really have any regrets about how I treat people or what I say to them.
Do you often feel like you're fidgeting or having trouble staying still when you're not at work?

Oh, my goodness, yes. It's actually driving my husband a little crazy, to be honest. You'd think, given what I do for a living—hauling freight, walking up and down those concrete staging lanes all day—that by the time I clock out, I'd just want to collapse. And usually, that's exactly how it is. I'm fifty-seven, you know, so a full shift on the docks usually leaves me pretty wiped out. 

But lately? After my shifts, instead of being worn out like usual, I come home and I'm just... buzzing. It's like I have this electricity humming right under my skin. I'll try to sit down in the living room—my husband always has the evening news or Jeopardy on when I get home—but sitting on the couch just feels completely impossible. My legs start jittering, my hands need to be doing something, and I feel like I'm going to crawl out of my skin if I don't get up. 

So I end up popping right back up. Just the other night, instead of relaxing, I spent hours completely reorganizing the kitchen cabinets. I took every single plate, bowl, and spice jar out, wiped down the wood, and rearranged everything by height. And when I finished that, I still couldn't settle down, so I went straight out to the garage and started sorting through all those big plastic storage bins we keep the holiday decorations in. I was pulling out the Christmas lights, untangling them, re-labeling the boxes with a permanent marker... I just couldn't stop moving. It makes absolutely no sense to have that much energy after a long shift on a hard warehouse floor, but I just cannot bring myself to just sit still.
Are you finding that your difficulties with focus and restlessness are affecting your daily relationships with your husband and others outside of work?

Well... yes. It really is, and I hate to admit it because I pride myself on keeping things running smoothly, but it’s definitely taking a toll. 

Even at work—which I know you asked about outside of work, but it really is bleeding into everything—I've actually been messing things up. I mentioned earlier how I know exactly what my priorities are with my clipboard, right? But because my focus just completely evaporates the second I hear a forklift backup alarm, I’ve been making actual inventory errors. Just last week, I wrote down that we had four pallets of the seasonal patio furniture when we only had two, and the other two were just regular garden soil that I hadn't looked closely enough at because I got distracted. I actually had to go and double-check everything with my supervisor, Dave. And Dave is a nice guy, he really is, but having to go to him and admit I couldn't trust my own counts? After doing this job for so long? It was humiliating. 

And then at home... well, with my husband, it’s just been really hard lately. He just retired, actually. He worked at the municipal water plant for thirty-five years, and this was supposed to be our time to sort of relax into that new phase of life, you know? He's got his knee issues, like I said, so he really just needs to rest and enjoy his evenings. But with me coming home and buzzing around like a trapped bee, tearing the kitchen cabinets apart at nine at night or sorting Christmas lights in the garage... it’s driving him up the wall. 

He’ll ask me to just sit down and watch a program with him, and I’ll tell him I *can't*, and then he gets frustrated, and then I get defensive because I feel like I'm crawling out of my skin and he doesn't understand it. We’ve been arguing so much over it. It’s gotten to the point where it feels like we’re just... walking around each other, you know? Tiptoeing around the house, trying to stay out of each other's way so we don't start another bicker, instead of actually settling into his retirement together like we planned. It just breaks my heart a little, honestly, because we usually get along so well, but right now it's just constant friction.
Are you finding it difficult to complete tasks at work due to your inability to focus?

Yes, exactly. In fact, that's really the main thing that pushed me to make this appointment in the first place—what brings me in today is just that I absolutely cannot keep my mind on one thing anymore. Like I was just telling you about that patio furniture mess, it is making it so incredibly hard to just finish my normal daily tasks. 

I’ll be standing there in the staging lane, right in the middle of a count, and I know exactly what I'm supposed to be doing. But then I'll hear a beeper from a delivery truck out on the dock, or a forklift alarm going off two aisles over, or even just someone moving a pallet and letting it scrape against the concrete... and it's like my brain just completely abandons what I'm doing. It pulls me right off the count. My head snaps over to whatever the noise is, and I completely lose my train of thought. 

And the worst part is, I'll keep going through the motions, and then a few minutes later I'll look down at my clipboard and realize I've put the completely wrong numbers into the inventory. It’s just so frustrating because I've been doing this for years, and I usually tune all that warehouse noise out. You have to, or you'd never get anything done! But lately, every single beeper, every single clatter, it just hijacks my attention. Then I have to start the whole count over from scratch, which slows everything down, or, heaven forbid, I don't catch it and I send a bad tally over to Dave. It's making a simple thirty-minute inventory check take over an hour because I just keep getting derailed by every little sound.
Are you finding that your difficulties with focus and restlessness are affecting your relationships with friends or family members beyond just your husband?

Well, to be honest, I haven't really noticed it causing too many issues with anyone else, mostly because I just haven't been seeing anyone else. My husband and I, we usually keep to ourselves anyway, especially since he retired. We have a few friends from his days at the water plant, and my sister lives about an hour away, but we don't see them all that often. 

My sister, actually, she called me last weekend—or was it the weekend before? The days are sort of blurring together lately with all this energy I have. But anyway, she called to catch up, and she did mention that I sounded a little out of breath or like I was rushing. But I was right in the middle of cleaning out the hall closet, which, let me tell you, was a disaster zone. I had pulled out all the winter coats and was sorting them by color, and then I realized half of them needed to go to the dry cleaners, so I was making a pile for that, and another pile for the donation bin. So I was just moving around a lot while we were on the phone. I don't think it bothered her, though. We just chatted for a few minutes and then she had to go run errands. 

And as for friends, like I said, we don't really do a lot of socializing during the week. By the time I get home from the warehouse, I'm usually—well, usually I'm exhausted, but lately, like I said, I'm just buzzing. But even with all this energy, I'm not really channeling it into going out or calling people. I'm just putting it into the house. It's just me and my husband here, so he's really the only one bearing the brunt of all this... whatever this is. This constant need to be moving and doing things. So, no, I wouldn't say it's affecting anyone else, just because there isn't really anyone else around to be affected by it, if that makes sense. It's really just the two of us, and Dave at work, dealing with the fallout.
Are you finding it challenging to enjoy your usual hobbies or activities due to your current state of mind?

Well, no, not really. I wouldn't say it's hard to enjoy them, exactly. If anything, I'm just doing them a lot more intensely? 

I know I mentioned earlier that I can't sit down and watch our evening programs with my husband anymore, which I guess used to be a nice little activity for us, but for my actual active hobbies... well, I'm still doing those. Like, my main hobby, the thing I really love to do when I'm not at the warehouse, is my garden. We have this big plot in the backyard, mostly raised cedar beds that my husband built for me a few years ago back when his knee was still holding up okay. I usually do tomatoes, bell peppers, some zucchini—though you know how zucchini is, it just completely takes over the whole box if you aren't careful and stay on top of it. 

Anyway, usually I just spend a couple of relaxing hours on a Sunday morning out there, pulling a few weeds, checking the soil, maybe putting down some fresh mulch. It’s supposed to be my quiet time. But lately, because I have all this... this buzzing energy I was telling you about, I’m out there at all hours. I was literally out there with a heavy-duty flashlight the other night. A flashlight! Just deadheading the marigolds and inspecting the tomato leaves for aphids at ten o'clock at night because I just couldn't stay inside and crawl out of my skin in the living room. 

So I'm definitely still enjoying the garden, I still love my plants, I really do. It's just that the way I'm doing it is completely different right now. I'm not sitting back on the patio chair and admiring the flowers with a cup of coffee like I used to. I'm treating the backyard like it's another warehouse staging lane that has to be perfectly sorted and managed right this very second. And I used to do a little knitting, too, mostly just scarves for my sister or the winter donation bins, but I haven't even touched my yarn basket lately because that requires sitting still. But the things I *can* do while I'm up and moving around? I'm still enjoying those just fine. Probably doing them a little too much, honestly, if you ask my husband.
Are you finding it difficult to manage your daily routines and responsibilities outside of work due to your current symptoms?

Well, it’s really bleeding into everything, to be honest. Outside of work, inside of work, it's all just getting so complicated and exhausting to manage. 

Since you asked about outside of work, the biggest thing is really the situation with my husband. I mean, we're supposed to be enjoying this time in our lives. He worked at the water plant for thirty-some years, his knees are pretty much shot, and this retirement was supposed to be our time to just finally settle in, you know? Have a quiet house, relax, maybe sit out on the patio he built. But instead, because I’m buzzing around like a hornet all the time and I can't just sit still with him, we are just constantly bickering. It’s not even always these big blow-out fights, it’s just this constant, exhausting friction. I’m up moving things around, he’s trying to rest, I’m getting snappy because he's just sitting there while I'm reorganizing the hall closet or whatever else I've gotten myself into... and now we've been arguing enough that it just feels like we’re constantly walking around each other in our own house. We're just avoiding each other instead of actually settling into his retirement together like we planned. It breaks my heart a little, but I just can't seem to stop moving long enough to fix it.

And honestly, it's not even just the routines at home that are a mess, because it carries right back over into my responsibilities at the warehouse, too. I know I was telling you earlier about the noises distracting me and messing up my counts? Well, it's gotten to the point where I’ve actually had to start going to my supervisor to double-check my work. Because of all those inventory errors I was making, I have to physically take my clipboard to Dave and have him look it over before I submit the final tally. It's just humiliating for someone who has been doing this job for as long as I have! I shouldn't need my boss to hold my hand to do a simple freight count. So, yes, managing just the basic day-to-day responsibilities, whether it's keeping the peace in my own marriage or just doing my normal stock tallies without needing a babysitter, it's all just become so incredibly difficult.
Do you feel like your current symptoms are affecting your overall happiness and well-being?

Well, happiness is a funny word to use for it right now, because honestly, it’s a real mixed bag. In some ways, I actually feel incredibly happy—but maybe too happy? Like, some days I wake up and I feel almost too upbeat, if that makes any sense at all. I get this feeling like I have an absolute engine inside me and I'm completely unstoppable. I'll get it in my head that I can fix up the entire house, completely reorganize all the closets, and then go into the warehouse and single-handedly sort out all of Dave's staging lanes, all before dinner time. 

I mean, just the other day I had this grand plan to pull up all the old shelving in the garage and build new ones from scratch, and it felt completely, one-hundred-percent doable. I felt fantastic about it! I was practically humming while I was measuring the walls. 

But then, that's where the well-being part really takes a hit, because it doesn't last. Or rather, it turns sour the second there's a roadblock. Because if my husband—who, bless his heart, is just trying to be practical since he's the one who'd probably have to help me with his bad knees—if he even just questions one of these big plans of mine, I just completely lose it. I snap at him, and I mean I really bite his head off over something incredibly small. He’ll just ask a simple, logical question like, "Where are we going to put the cars while you build these shelves?" and it’s like a switch flips. I go from feeling on top of the world to just being so incredibly irritable and angry that he isn't matching my energy. 

And then, of course, after I snap at him, he gets quiet, and we're right back to that awful friction and walking on eggshells around each other that I was telling you about. So I'm riding this huge, productive high where I feel great, but the second he questions me, I turn into a snapping turtle. So, no, I wouldn't say my overall well-being is in a good place, because living on this kind of rollercoaster where I'm overly upbeat one minute and completely irritable the next... well, it's just draining the life out of our home.
Are you feeling like your current state is affecting your ability to maintain a healthy and fulfilling relationship with your husband and others?

Well, I mean, I know I already talked your ear off about my husband, but yes, it really is taking a toll there. It is just so hard because, like I was saying, thirty years he spent at that water plant!
